planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; acai palm is a frost-tender floodplain species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse with high humidity.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; acai palm is a frost-tender floodplain species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse with high humidity. Native to the seasonally flooded várzea forests of the Amazon River basin, this multi-stemmed, clustering palm produces heavy clusters of small, dark purple, antioxidant-rich berries that are pulped fresh into the acai bowls and juices that have become a global health-food phenomenon, though the fruit itself is highly perishable and must be processed within a day of harvest. It thrives in wet, swampy, even periodically flooded soil unlike most palms, reflecting its floodplain origin, and forms multiple clustering trunks over time rather than a single stem. Water generously and consistently, since it does not tolerate drought, and expect several years of growth before the first fruit clusters are produced.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently wet soil at a pond or wetland margin in full sun; buriti palm is a frost-tender wetland species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11 and grows naturally standing in shallow water.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, consistently wet soil at a pond or wetland margin in full sun; buriti palm is a frost-tender wetland species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11 and grows naturally standing in shallow water. One of the most iconic palms of the Amazon basin and Venezuelan and Colombian llanos wetlands, it forms dense stands, called buritizais, in permanently waterlogged swamp forest, its tall, solitary trunk topped with a crown of large fan-shaped fronds and heavy clusters of reddish-brown, scaly-skinned fruit prized fresh or processed into juice, oil, and traditional foods across the Amazon region. It is an exceptionally slow-growing, long-lived palm that needs many years, often a decade or more, before reaching fruiting maturity, and its dependence on permanently wet or flooded soil makes it unsuitable for anything but a wetland or pond-margin planting. Provide constant moisture or standing water at the roots and full sun, and be prepared for a very long wait before any fruit harvest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bacuri is a frost-tender Amazonian tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; bacuri is a frost-tender Amazonian tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the Amazon and Brazilian cerrado regions, this large forest tree produces a thick-shelled, yellow fruit containing creamy, tangy-sweet white pulp considered one of the finest-flavored fruits of the Amazon, used fresh and in ice creams, juices, and preserves across northern Brazil, though the tree is notoriously slow to reach fruiting age. A relative of mangosteen in the same plant family, it shares that group's exacting climate requirements and very long juvenile period, often a decade or more before first fruiting, making it a specialty tree for dedicated tropical fruit collectors and botanical gardens rather than a quick home orchard planting. Water regularly during the long establishment period, and provide the warm, humid, consistently frost-free conditions the tree requires to eventually bear fruit.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Amazon grape is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Amazon grape is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the western Amazon basin, this fast-growing relative of cecropia trees bears grape-like clusters of purple, thin-skinned fruit with sweet, translucent, juicy pulp eaten fresh, unusual among tropical fruit trees for reaching bearing age within just a few years of planting rather than a decade or more. Its palmate, cecropia-like leaves and relatively quick growth to fruiting make it an appealing option for a tropical fruit collector wanting faster results than many slower Amazonian species, though it still needs consistent warmth and humidity to thrive. Water regularly, especially during establishment, and expect the first fruit clusters within three to five years under good growing conditions.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chullpi quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather.

directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chullpi quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather. A traditional Andean landrace distinct from the more familiar white, red, and black quinoa sold commercially, this variety is prized in its native Peru and Bolivia for translucent, pale golden seed with a naturally sweet flavor reminiscent of corn, traditionally toasted and eaten as a snack rather than cooked as a grain like standard quinoa. It grows on tall, colorful seed-head spikes typical of quinoa and is naturally low in the bitter seed coating (saponin) found on many quinoa varieties, requiring less rinsing before cooking or toasting. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before storing or toasting.
sources: Slow Food International Ark of Taste
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; wild achocha grows and fruits quickly through a single warm season.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; wild achocha grows and fruits quickly through a single warm season. A fast-growing Andean relative of the more widely grown achocha (Cyclanthera pedata), it produces smaller, spiny, hollow, cucumber-flavored fruit on vigorous tendril-climbing vines, harvested young and cooked or pickled much like its better-known relative, with a similarly mild, crunchy texture. Extremely productive and easy from seed, it thrives in ordinary garden soil with a support to climb and can produce a heavy crop of small fruit within two to three months of sowing in warm weather. Harvest fruit young, while still tender and before seeds mature and harden, for the best eating quality, and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive through the season.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
Slow Food International Ark of Taste
